title: Crossing the ocean
hook: the world is an ocean hard to cross; Nanak says attention on the Word carries you over

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis asked Nanak who his guru was, and he said the Word is the Guru, attention the disciple. Your line was the word is guru. Did you give something true your full attention? Day one thousand one hundred forty.

Dutar. Hard to cross. That's how the yogi Charpat describes the world when he puts his question to Nanak, near the start of the Sidh Gosht. The world is an ocean, he says, and they call it hard to cross. How does anyone reach the far shore? Six days ago we heard half of the answer, the duck that swims the stream and stays dry. But the duck was only the first move. Charpat asked about crossing, and the stanza doesn't leave him in the water. Today: crossing the ocean, and what carries a person over.
screen: `DUTAR: HARD TO CROSS.` → `CHARPAT'S OCEAN.` → `THE DUCK WAS HALF THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest of the stanza, in paraphrase. With attention fixed on the Word, the terrifying world-ocean is crossed, says Nanak, by speaking the Name. The phrase for the world-ocean is bhav saagar. Saagar is the sea. Bhav is the world of becoming, the churn of being born, wanting, losing, wanting again. Notice that Nanak accepts the yogi's picture. He doesn't say the world is a calm pond or that Charpat is exaggerating. The water really is deep, and the waves are real. What he changes is the way across. One way is to climb above the water, onto a peak where the waves can't reach. Nanak's answer goes through it. Attention resting on the Word is what holds a person up while they cross. Elsewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru and the Name are pictured as a boat or a ship. That fills in the picture: the world is the ocean, the Word is the boat. And the picture is honest about a few things. A boat doesn't make the sea smaller. The storm still comes. You still get wet, sometimes very wet. But a person in a boat isn't fighting the water with their own arms. They're held by something built for the crossing. And put this beside yesterday. Attention tuned to the Word was the disciple. Today, attention fixed on the Word is how the disciple crosses. It's the same attention, doing two jobs: learning, and staying afloat. On a bad night, when the waves are high, that may be all a person has. One line, held. In this stanza, that's enough to carry someone over. The word is the boat.
screen: `BHAV SAAGAR: THE WORLD-OCEAN.` · `NANAK ACCEPTS THE DEEP WATER.` · `ATTENTION ON THE WORD CARRIES.` · `THE BOAT DOESN'T SHRINK THE SEA.` · then, large: `THE WORD IS THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at water and breathe. Find some water you can see: a glass on the table, a sink, rain on a window, or just the memory of a lake or the sea. Let your eyes rest on it. Notice how it moves, or how still it is. Then let the breath come and go like small waves. Bring to mind one thing that feels deep or rough in your life right now. Don't try to calm it. Just picture yourself held above it, and give your attention one line to rest on: Waheguru, or today's line, the word is the boat. If you pray, you can let that line carry the weight for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Crossing the ocean. Charpat's question about the world-ocean, hard to cross, and Nanak's answer: with attention on the Word, a person crosses over. Today's word.
Your line: the word is the boat. Each time you touch water today, washing your hands, a drink, the shower, let your line come back and hold you for one breath. Day one thousand one hundred forty.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the world as bhav saagar, the world-ocean, and of the Guru's Word and the Name as what carries a person across; the image returns in Gurbani sung in kirtan.

fork.setup: you're in deep water and the far shore is a long way off. Charpat asks how anyone crosses. what does the stanza say carries you?
options: swimming harder on your own strength.
waiting on the shore until the sea is calm.
fork.reveal: with attention on the Word, the world-ocean is crossed, says the stanza, by speaking the Name.

original.note: saagar: the sea; with bhav, the world-ocean Charpat calls hard to cross.

trapdoor: what you thought: to escape the world's storms you need to get out of the water.
what it means: Nanak says attention fixed on the Word carries a person across the world-ocean.
what a scholar hears: the stanza takes the shared Indic image of crossing the bhav saagar and makes the shabad, not ascetic withdrawal, the means.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali, Mahala 1, Sidh Gosht, pauris 4–5, Ang 938 (Charpat's question; surat sabad bhav saagar tareeai)

notes: Pauri 5 paraphrased (dunee-aa saagar dutar kaheeai; surat sabad bhav saagar tareeai, naanak naam vakhaanai). Day 1134 used the lotus and duck from the same stanza; this day uses its crossing line. Please confirm.
Gloss of bhav (the world of becoming, birth and wanting) and saagar (sea) given as meanings, not etymology; please confirm.
'Elsewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru and the Name are pictured as a boat or a ship' is not tied to a specific Ang; a Keeper may wish to add one (e.g., the bohith/jahaaj images).
